Confession time: I used to fly fixed-wing jets in the Air Force a (very) long time ago. I'm in the "Supersonic" club... I'm in the "I've flown upside-down" club. (I am NOT in the "Mile High" club, however.) This isn't the first time this has happened, although it IS the first time such drastic measures have been taken (at least since the ramp up in WW2). The problem is the training cycle and the myopic way the Air Force conducts it. It takes about a year to put someone through all the phases of Undergraduate Pilot Training (UPT) to get pilot wings, and that only gets those who graduate into the pipeline to go to another lengthy course (or series of them) before they're ready to fly real-world missions. There are bottlenecks at every stage, and the Air Force washes people out of the courses if there aren't enough cockpits to put them into in the next phase right at that moment in time. I've seen it happen... more than a few times. It's incredibly wasteful, and the Air Force has trained (or partially-trained) thousands of guys who could easily be flying right now, but aren't because they permanently took them off flying status due to the short-term availability of cockpits at the next stage.

Something similar happened around the time of the first Gulf War... the Clinton Administration had cut the military eight years in a row. The cumulative effect was immense, and our adversaries started to perceive us as being weak. Weakness invites aggression, and Iraq figured we wouldn't defend our ally Kuwait if they invaded them... which they did. The Air Force was desperate for pilots and put on a full-court press to get guys in the air once Congress gave the green light to push the Iraqis back over the border.

The long-term good news is that manned fighting aircraft are going the way of the catapult and the broadsword because of emerging technology (a lot of combat missions are already being flown by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs)). You can build a plane that can make a 50-g turn, but you can't get a manned plane to go past about 8 or 9g (and then only for a few seconds), because the pilot can't take more than that without "graying out" or even "blacking out" (ask me how I know).

In fact, the future of aerial combat may involve fat dudes sitting in comfy chairs piloting supersonic wonder-machines by remote control, because the only physical activity they've ever done involves sitting in comfy chairs playing video games their entire lives. Realistically, though, those machines will be too fast for people to "keep up with" at all, and most of their flight controls will be run by computers, with human input only at critical stages like "Shoot - Don't Shoot."
